::: {.callout-note}
## [AQUA]{.acronym-literal} Version 2 ([AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal})

This is **Version 2** of the interactive research artifact, now named **[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal}**.

[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} builds on the original **[AQUA]{.acronym-literal}** quality modeling framework [1] and extends it in two major ways.

First, the conceptualization of authentication quality is refined. Quality previously attributed to an **Authenticator Employment** is now modeled as **Authentication Technique Quality**. An Authenticator Employment defines how authenticators are composed, while an Authentication Technique represents the concrete composition of authenticators that is implemented by an Authentication Solution [2].

Second, [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} extends the previously definitional [AQUA]{.acronym-literal} quality models [1] with **quality prediction models**. For each quality subfactor, prediction metrics are defined that enable authentication qualities to be assessed and compared. Ordinal quality levels are normalized to the interval **[0, 1]** to make different quality assessments comparable [3].

[View [AQUA]{.acronym-literal} Version 1](https://aqua-authentication.github.io/AQUA/)
:::

Welcome to the [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} Webpage.

Authentication is one of the most widely used security controls [4]. It is the process by which a user verifies the identity they claim using one or more **authenticators** [5], such as a password or fingerprint. The conceptual approach used to perform authentication is an **authentication technique** [2], while the key design, architectural, and implementation choices made to realize authentication form an **authentication solution** [6].

[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} builds on [AQUA]{.acronym-literal}, a modular quality modeling framework for authentication solutions [1]. Its modular approach allows authentication quality to be considered at different levels. Authenticators have inherent quality properties, authentication techniques are affected by the authenticators they employ and their composition, and authentication solutions additionally depend on their concrete implementation.

[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} applies this framework to **quality prediction** by defining quality prediction models for **Authenticators**, **Authentication Techniques**, and **Authentication Solutions**. These models enable authentication qualities to be assessed and compared.

# Authentication Quality Concepts {#authentication-quality-concepts .unnumbered}

[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} builds on the modular [AQUA]{.acronym-literal} framework [1], which decomposes authentication into four interrelated concepts: **Authenticator**, **Authenticator Employment**, **Authentication Technique**, and **Authentication Solution**.

An **Authenticator** is the fundamental entity a user possesses, controls, and uses to perform authentication, such as a password or fingerprint.

An **Authenticator Employment** defines the composition scheme of authenticators in terms of their cardinality, mode, and order.

An **Authentication Technique** is the concrete composition of one or more authenticators that conforms to an Authenticator Employment.

An **Authentication Solution** comprises the key design, architectural, and implementation choices made to realize authentication. One part of an Authentication Solution is the Authentication Technique it implements.

Authenticators, Authentication Techniques, and Authentication Solutions each have distinct qualities. These qualities propagate from the **Authenticator**, over its composition within an **Authentication Technique**, to its concrete implementation as an **Authentication Solution**. While an Authenticator Employment determines how authenticators are composed and thereby affects Authentication Technique Quality, the resulting quality is attributed to the Authentication Technique.

![The refined [AQUA]{.acronym-literal} concept framework [1] underlying [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal}. Solid edges depict concepts; dashed edges represent instantiations.](figures/concepts-with-technique.svg){.concept-model-image}

Credentials bind an authenticator to a user’s identity. They are not represented as a separate concept in this artifact, but distinguishing credentials from authenticators is relevant when considering availability properties.

# [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} Quality Model Overview {#aquaedict-quality-model-overview}

::: {.callout-note}
## Research Status

[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} represents the current state of the research and may be further refined in future versions.
:::

[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} distinguishes three fundamental levels of authentication quality: **Authenticator Quality**, **Authentication Technique Quality**, and **Authentication Solution Quality**. These qualities build on each other from the atomic level of an Authenticator, over the composition of Authenticators in an Authentication Technique, to the concrete implementation of an Authentication Solution.

The original [AQUA]{.acronym-literal} framework introduced the quality models [AQUA-A]{.acronym-literal}, [AQUA-E]{.acronym-literal}, and [AQUA-S]{.acronym-literal} [1]. In [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal}, the middle quality level is refined: the quality previously attributed to an **Authenticator Employment** is now attributed to the **Authentication Technique**. While an Authenticator Employment determines how Authenticators are composed and therefore affects their resulting quality, the actual manifestation of this quality is inherent to the Authentication Technique.

Based on these three quality levels, [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} defines three corresponding quality prediction models:

- **[AQUÆDICT-A]{.acronym-literal}** for Authenticators
- **[AQUÆDICT-T]{.acronym-literal}** for Authentication Techniques
- **[AQUÆDICT-S]{.acronym-literal}** for Authentication Solutions

![Overview of the [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} quality models and their quality-factor dependencies.](figures/aqua-models.svg){.concept-model-image}


# Quality Prediction Models

::: {.callout-note}
## Work in Progress

The quality prediction models presented in [AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} reflect the current state of the research. The proposed prediction metrics are intended to demonstrate the overall approach and may be further refined and evaluated in future versions.
:::

## Prediction Metrics

[AQUÆDICT]{.acronym-literal} extends the definitional quality models of [AQUA]{.acronym-literal} [1] with **quality prediction models** for **Authenticators**, **Authentication Techniques**, and **Authentication Solutions**. These are represented by [AQUÆDICT-A]{.acronym-literal}, [AQUÆDICT-T]{.acronym-literal}, and [AQUÆDICT-S]{.acronym-literal}, respectively.

For each quality subfactor, a **prediction metric** is defined. The metrics are based on quality rankings defined by the inherent properties of the Authenticators.

For an ordinal scale with $k$ quality levels,

$$
L_k = \{l_0 < l_1 < \dots < l_{k-1}\}
$$

the levels are ordered from the worst quality level $l_0$ to the best quality level $l_{k-1}$. At the Authenticator level, the corresponding quality prediction function for a quality subfactor $q$ is defined as

$$
Q_q : A \rightarrow L_{k_q}
$$

where $A$ is an Authenticator and $k_q$ is the number of quality levels defined for the respective subfactor.

## Normalization

To make ordinal quality assessments comparable with cardinal subfactors, the ordinal scales are normalized to the interval **[0, 1]** using an established normalization approach from multi-criteria decision analysis [3].

$$
\operatorname{norm}(l_i) = \frac{i}{k_q - 1}
$$

The normalization assigns **0** to the worst quality level and **1** to the best quality level, independent of the number of levels used by a particular quality subfactor. This provides a common scale on which different quality assessments can be compared.
